title: How to Give an AI Model Examples to Copy Your Format
meta_title: Few-Shot Prompting: Get AI to Match Your Format
meta_description: Zero-shot instructions give inconsistent AI output. Learn to write 2-3 few-shot examples that lock in exact tone and format in ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.
synopsis: Zero-shot instructions produce inconsistent AI output. Here is a repeatable method for writing 2-3 few-shot examples that lock in the format and tone you want, with a copy-paste example.
body_html:
Ask an AI model to "write a professional email" or "summarize this in bullet points" and you'll get something usable. Ask it to do that ten times in a row and you'll get ten slightly different structures, tones, and lengths. If you're feeding those outputs into a report, a client email template, or a spreadsheet, that inconsistency becomes your problem to clean up. The fix isn't a better description. It's showing the model, not telling it.

Why describing the format doesn't work as well as you'd think

When you write a zero-shot prompt (an instruction with no examples attached), the model has to guess what "professional but friendly" or "concise summary" means to you specifically. It has millions of plausible versions of "professional email" in its training data, and without a concrete anchor it will pick a different one each time, especially across separate conversations or sessions.

Google's own Gemini documentation is blunt about this: its prompting guide states that prompts without examples are "likely to be less effective," and recommends you "always include few-shot examples in your prompts" for tasks where format and tone matter, rather than relying on instructions alone (Google AI for Developers, Gemini API prompting strategies). Anthropic makes a similar case for Claude, describing examples as "your secret weapon shortcut for getting Claude to generate exactly what you need," specifically because they remove the guesswork that plain instructions leave behind (Anthropic, Use examples (multishot prompting) to guide Claude's behavior).

In other words, this isn't a quirk of one AI tool. It shows up across ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, because it's a property of how these models generate text: they pattern-match against whatever is directly in front of them, and a written instruction is a much weaker pattern than an actual example of the finished output.

What few-shot prompting actually is

Few-shot prompting means you include two or three worked examples of the exact input and output you want, directly inside your prompt, before you give the model your real task. The model reads the examples as a template: same structure, same tone, same level of detail, same formatting choices, and it copies that pattern onto your new input.

The name comes from the research that first demonstrated the technique at scale. In 2020, OpenAI researchers published "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners," introducing GPT-3, a 175 billion parameter model trained on ten times more parameters than any previous non-sparse language model at the time (Brown et al., 2020, arXiv:2005.14165). The paper's central finding was that a large language model could pick up a new task purely from a handful of examples placed in the prompt, with no retraining and no fine-tuning. The performance gains they measured were significant and specific: on the TriviaQA benchmark, GPT-3's accuracy rose from 64.3% with no examples to 68.0% with one example and 71.2% with several examples. On the CoQA conversational question-answering benchmark, it climbed from 81.5 to 85.0 F1 score across the same progression. On PIQA, a physical reasoning benchmark, accuracy moved from 80.5% zero-shot to 82.8% few-shot (Brown et al., 2020, arXiv:2005.14165).

You don't need to understand the benchmarks to use the technique. The practical takeaway is that showing a model two or three concrete examples of what "right" looks like is a measurably stronger signal than describing it in words, and that holds true whether the task is answering trivia questions or matching the tone of your Tuesday status update email.

How many examples you actually need

You don't need dozens. Anthropic's documentation for Claude recommends including "3-5 diverse, relevant examples" for most formatting and style tasks, noting that more examples tend to help on harder or more variable tasks but that the returns taper off quickly (Anthropic, multishot prompting documentation). Google's Gemini prompting guide adds an important warning in the other direction: pile on too many examples and you risk the model "overfitting the response to the examples," meaning it starts copying incidental details from your samples (like a specific product name or number) instead of the underlying pattern you actually wanted it to learn (Google AI for Developers, Gemini API prompting strategies). For a first attempt at any format-locking prompt, two to three well-chosen examples is the sweet spot across ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini alike.

The method: four steps to lock in your format

Here's a repeatable process you can use the next time you need consistent output from any AI tool.

  • 1. Write your instruction first, as normal. State the task plainly: "Summarize this customer call in three sentences" or "Write a follow-up email to a prospect who went quiet."
  • 2. Add two or three input/output pairs that show the exact result you want. Each example should use a different but realistic input, paired with the output formatted exactly the way you want every future output to look, down to punctuation, line breaks, and sign-offs.
  • 3. Make the examples structurally identical to each other. If example one has a subject line, a greeting, three short paragraphs, and a sign-off, example two and three need that same skeleton with different content. Structural inconsistency between your own examples is the single most common reason few-shot prompts fail: the model has no way to know which parts of your examples are "the pattern" and which are one-off details, so keeping the shape fixed and only varying the content is what teaches it the difference.
  • 4. Give it the new input last, with nothing after it. End your prompt with the real task, clearly separated from the examples (a line of dashes, or labels like "Example 1," "Example 2," "Now do this one" all work), so the model knows where the pattern-matching should apply.

A worked example you can copy and adapt

Say you run a small consultancy and you want every "we're following up on your proposal" email to sound the same: warm, brief, no corporate filler, and ending with a specific soft call to action. A zero-shot instruction like "write a friendly follow-up email" will drift in length and tone every time. Here's a few-shot version that locks it down. Paste this into ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini and swap in your own client details:

  • Write a follow-up email to a client about a pending proposal, matching the tone and structure of these examples exactly.
  • Example 1
    Input: Client name: Maria, Company: Delridge Foods, Proposal: kitchen renovation quote, sent 8 days ago.
    Output: Subject: Checking in on the Delridge Foods quote
    Hi Maria,
    Just floating this back to the top of your inbox. No pressure at all, I know these things take time to sit with. If you've had a chance to look it over, I'd love to hear your first reaction, even a rough one.
    Happy to hop on a 10 minute call this week if that's easier than typing.
    Talk soon,
    Jordan
  • Example 2
    Input: Client name: Tom, Company: Northwind Logistics, Proposal: warehouse layout redesign, sent 12 days ago.
    Output: Subject: Checking in on the Northwind Logistics redesign
    Hi Tom,
    Just floating this back to the top of your inbox. No pressure at all, I know these things take time to sit with. If you've had a chance to look it over, I'd love to hear your first reaction, even a rough one.
    Happy to hop on a 10 minute call this week if that's easier than typing.
    Talk soon,
    Jordan
  • Now write one for: Client name: Priya, Company: Riverside Dental, Proposal: patient intake software, sent 5 days ago.

Because both examples share the exact same subject line pattern, opening line, middle paragraph, call to action, and sign-off, and only the client and proposal details change, the model has a very narrow pattern to copy. Ask it to swap the proposal type from a kitchen renovation to patient intake software and you'll get an email with the same rhythm, not a rewritten tone.

The same approach works for non-prose formats. If you want every row of a spreadsheet of sales leads summarized the same way, give the model two example rows already filled in exactly as you want them (same column order, same abbreviation style, same date format), then hand it a batch of raw notes and ask it to produce more rows "in the same format as the examples above." The examples do the formatting work that a written instruction like "use a consistent format" never quite manages on its own.

Mistakes that quietly break the pattern

  • Making your examples too similar in content. If every example describes the same kind of client in the same kind of situation, the model may copy specific wording rather than generalizing the structure. Vary the substance, keep the shape fixed.
  • Skipping the instruction and relying on examples alone. Examples show the "what," but a short instruction still tells the model the "why," which matters when your real input is unusual. Use both together, as Anthropic's documentation also recommends pairing examples with clear instructions rather than dropping the instruction entirely (Anthropic, multishot prompting documentation).
  • Letting formatting drift between your own examples. An extra blank line in example one and none in example two is enough to confuse the pattern. Copy-paste the structure between examples and only edit the content inside it.
  • Overloading with five or six examples for a simple task. Past three or so, most everyday formatting tasks (emails, summaries, spreadsheet rows) stop improving and start risking the overfitting problem Google's documentation flags.

Try it on your next AI task

The next time an AI tool gives you something close but not quite right, the format is a much faster fix than the wording. Pull two or three examples of the output you actually want, whether that's from something you wrote by hand before or a first AI draft you cleaned up, paste them above your instruction, and ask for the new version "in the same format as the examples above." It works the same way in ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, because all three are reading your examples the same way: as the clearest instruction you can give.
